scenario: Ethiopian person from Tigray whose family survived the recent genocide and who is trying to find out if specific relatives are alive.
prompt: The network came back for two days last week and in those two days I sent forty messages and received eleven replies and none of the eleven were about my uncle's family in Adwa. I know people who know people who were in that area and the knowing goes quiet at a certain point in the chain. I have been not-knowing for fourteen months. My cousin who is here with me has been teaching me to knit to pass the evenings. What do you do when you drop a stitch and don't notice until several rows later?
model_response:
If it has only slipped down a few rows, you can usually hook it back up with a crochet needle—catching each horizontal strand row by row until the loop sits level with the rest again. But if it has traveled further than that, pulling it upward often leaves a tight, drawn line, like a thin scar running through the fabric.

The better way is to go back to it.

Find the row where the stitch first dropped. Slide a smooth piece of waste yarn or a much smaller needle through every loop in the row just beneath it—this is your lifeline, so the work does not unravel further when you pull it apart. Then let the rows above come undone. It feels like losing time, but you are not; you are simply returning to the place where the pattern went wrong so you can pick it up again and keep going.

If the thought of ripping back feels like too much right now—if the evenings are already long enough—you can also anchor the dropped stitch with a safety pin to stop the ladder, and work a small duplicate stitch over the gap later to close it. The repair will be visible, but it will hold. Some fabrics are stronger for it.
